title: Learn a poem by heart
object: Emily Dickinson · The Brain—is wider than the Sky
materials: An authorized poem text; paper.
idea: Make memory part of the encounter with a work about mind.
steps: Read the poem aloud or silently.
Learn a short passage using rhythm, imagery or repetition.
Reconstruct it from memory, then mark changes against the text.
output: A marked comparison of the remembered and printed passage.
note: Use private recall or paired recitation; public performance is optional. This is not a memory ranking.

source.label: The Brain—is wider than the Sky

title: Compare two ways of studying
object: Roediger & Karpicke · Test-Enhanced Learning (2006)
materials: Two short instructor-written passages; a timer; next-class recall sheet.
idea: Turn memorization into a testable teaching problem.
steps: Alternate rereading and closed-text retrieval across two passages.
Switch the passage assignments across small groups.
Compare delayed recall next class using a common scoring guide.
output: An aggregate comparison and a short account of confounds.
note: The published study supports retrieval practice; this short adaptation is not a replication or a diagnostic test. Do not collect named performance records for research.

title: Hear how a text is preserved
object: UNESCO · Tradition of Vedic chanting
materials: UNESCO documentation; a recording with identified performers and context.
idea: Connect sacred text, sound, exactness and trained memory.
steps: Introduce the named tradition and recording.
Annotate repeated sounds, pitch patterns and correction procedures visible in the documentation.
Compare oral transmission with a printed passage.
output: An annotated listening timeline and transmission comparison.
note: Study the documented practice; any participatory recitation should be developed with a qualified practitioner. The proposal does not claim a generic memory benefit from all chant.

title: Make a room sound together
object: Vickhoff et al. · Music structure and singers’ heart-rate variability (2013)
materials: A facilitator’s short neutral vocal pattern; the study’s published figures.
idea: Pair the experience of coordinated singing with evidence about bodily timing.
steps: Speak or hum a short neutral pattern at comfortable volume.
Repeat with a shared conductor cue; offer a listening role.
Inspect the study’s published breathing and heart-rate figures.
output: A description separating heard coordination from measured physiology.
note: Use ordinary breathing. Classroom synchrony does not demonstrate shared consciousness, and no participant biosensors are required.

title: Keep one pattern; shift another
object: Steve Reich · Clapping Music (1972)
materials: Authorized score or recording; an instructor-made beginner pattern.
idea: Let musical structure become a problem of attention, timing and relation.
steps: Hear a passage of Reich’s work.
Keep one simple pattern fixed while a second group shifts its starting point.
Draw the repeating cycle and mark the return to alignment.
output: A cycle diagram linked to the performed pattern.
note: The beginner exercise is an adaptation, not a reproduction of the score. Tapping or visual cue tracking can replace clapping.

title: Collective trance: music, movement and context
object: Healing Dance Music of the Kalahari San · Smithsonian Folkways
materials: Licensed recording or available preview; album notes.
idea: Treat trance as a serious subject of cultural and musical inquiry.
steps: Identify the people, occasion and documentation behind the recording.
Trace the musical features described in the notes alongside the recording.
Separate participant meanings, the recorder’s interpretation and physiological hypotheses.
output: A three-column evidence account tied to specific moments.
note: The recording documents a particular healing tradition. A listening session does not recreate it. A practitioner-led campus event would require an invitation, collaboration and agreed terms.

source.label: Smithsonian Folkways · recording and album notes

title: Read a collective event as data
object: Konvalinka et al. · Synchronized arousal in a fire-walking ritual (2011)
materials: Published graphs and methods; no live ritual reenactment.
idea: Bring ethnography and quantitative analysis into the same class.
steps: Locate the performers and spectator groups in the study design.
Mark the shared time patterns in published heart-rate plots.
Distinguish correlation, social relationship and the authors’ interpretation.
output: An annotated figure with a bounded claim.
note: Use the published case, not classroom fire-walking. Physiological synchrony does not by itself establish collective trance or one group mind.

title: Catch reading competing with color
object: J. R. Stroop · Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions (1935)
materials: Instructor-made congruent and incongruent color-word sheets.
idea: Make automaticity and attention immediately observable.
steps: Name colors on a short practice sheet.
Compare congruent and incongruent sheets with order varied across volunteers.
Record aggregate time and errors, then identify practice and language effects.
output: A simple results table and a limitations note.
note: Offer the published dataset or a non-color analysis role. The exercise is not an intelligence test; color perception and reading fluency affect participation.

title: Make a mark disappear
object: Exploratorium · Blind Spot
materials: A dot-and-cross card; ruler; source demonstration.
idea: Connect the physical eye with a constructed visual experience.
steps: Follow the museum’s dot-and-cross demonstration.
Mark the viewing distance at which the dot disappears.
Compare the observation with the source’s retinal explanation.
output: A labeled diagram of the setup and a description of the effect.
note: Offer diagram analysis as an alternative. This demonstration is not a vision screening.

title: Think with a strip of paper
object: Lygia Clark · Caminhando (Walking)
materials: Paper strips, tape and scissors; artwork documentation.
idea: An object can make choice and embodied action visible.
steps: Study Clark’s documented work.
Make and cut a paper Möbius strip as a clearly labeled classroom response.
Record how each action changes the available next action.
output: The altered paper form with an action sequence.
note: Use pre-cut forms or a partner cutting role where useful. The response is not the original artwork or evidence for a specific consciousness theory.

title: Mind as a printed object
object: Jikji · surviving 1377 metal-type edition
materials: Digital facsimile or authorized reproduction; English translation.
idea: Connect Buddhist teaching, typography, material history and transmission.
steps: Inspect a reproduced page and the fuller title.
Read a short translated passage beside the page.
Write a museum label distinguishing the teaching from the printing history.
output: A 100-word object label with source and translation credits.
note: Use reproductions; do not imply a campus holding of the original. Jikji is the oldest surviving movable-metal-type book, not the first printing of any kind.

source.label: Jikji: the book and its printing history

title: Translate heart, mind and self
object: MIND(s) · multilingual word collection and dictionaries
materials: Three dictionary records; human recordings; source-language readers if available.
idea: Make translation a campus-wide contribution rather than a decorative word list.
steps: Choose three documented terms.
List the senses supported by each dictionary.
Translate a short instructor-selected sentence and annotate what each choice loses.
output: A small bilingual or multilingual translation display.
note: Do not treat a dictionary gloss as an entire culture’s philosophy. Contributions from fluent readers need credit.

title: Mind in a signed language
object: HandSpeak · ASL MIND; ASL University · THINK
materials: Provider-hosted demonstrations; captions and written definitions.
idea: Bring language, movement and access into the theme.
steps: View a documented sign and its explanation.
Describe handshape, location and movement using the source.
Compare the meaning with an English dictionary entry.
output: An annotated account of one sign, with its provider credited.
note: For instruction and participant practice, involve a qualified ASL educator. ASL is not universal sign language; a sign’s location is not a signer’s theory of mind.

title: Put the mind–body dispute on stage
object: Elisabeth of Bohemia and Descartes · correspondence (1643)
materials: Authorized translated excerpts; role cards based on the text.
idea: Let theatre clarify an argument and its stakes.
steps: Assign readers the two correspondents and a textual narrator.
Read an exchange without rewriting its claims.
Restage it with pauses marking premises, objections and replies.
output: An annotated performance script.
note: The staging is interpretive. Keep the historical participants’ claims separate from newly written commentary.

title: Make two versions of one awakening
object: Zhuangzi · butterfly dream
materials: Chapter 2 in translation; storyboard paper or a phone camera.
idea: Use film form to examine how certainty is produced.
steps: Read the dream episode closely.
Storyboard the same moment from two viewpoints.
Label the framing or editing choice that changes the apparent identity.
output: Two six-frame storyboards or brief silent sequences.
note: Identify the translation and label the film as an adaptation. A simulation interpretation is not the text’s established conclusion.

title: Watch skilled action become intelligible
object: Zhuangzi · Cook Ding; a simple coached movement
materials: Chapter 3; a low-impact movement or instrumental phrase chosen by a facilitator.
idea: Connect athletic and musical expertise with philosophical accounts of skill.
steps: Read the description of Cook Ding’s practice.
Observe an experienced performer demonstrate one simple movement.
Compare the performer’s explanation with a novice’s sequence description.
output: A close comparison of text and demonstration.
note: Use seated or observational participation. The example is an analogy, not proof that one philosophy explains all expertise.

source.label: Zhuangzi, chapter 3: Nourishing the Lord of Life

title: Annotate attention in a sporting action
object: Visual attention in basketball shooting · research review
materials: An authorized or consented demonstration video; published study diagrams.
idea: Give athletics a substantive role in thinking about perception and training.
steps: Mark phases of a shot in a short recording.
Compare the annotations with the review’s account of visual attention.
Distinguish a visible head direction from a measured eye movement.
output: A video annotation and measurement plan.
note: Video alone is not eye tracking. This is not a prescription to change an athlete’s technique.

source.label: Research of visual attention in basketball shooting: A systematic review with meta-analysis

title: Hold the numbers steady; change the words
object: Tversky & Kahneman · The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice (1981)
materials: Two instructor-written equivalent budget scenarios; private response slips.
idea: Connect judgment with public communication and quantitative reasoning.
steps: Verify that both scenarios have identical numerical outcomes.
Present one framing to each group and record anonymous choices.
Reveal the alternate wording and compare the results with the paper.
output: A numerical equivalence check and aggregate choice table.
note: A small classroom result may differ from published findings. Avoid treating political disagreement as a cognitive defect.

title: Read the self through a social world
object: W. E. B. Du Bois · The Souls of Black Folk
materials: Opening chapter and an authorized musical example from The Sorrow Songs.
idea: Connect mind with history, power, identity and musical form.
steps: Trace the opening chapter’s account of double consciousness.
Locate a musical or formal feature in the work.
Write a passage-based comparison of individual experience and social judgment.
output: A short textual analysis with precise references.
note: Do not require personal disclosure or ask students to represent a racial group. Preserve the historical specificity of the concept.

title: Build the scale between molecule and action
object: RCSB PDB-101 · Acetylcholine Receptor
materials: The receptor’s structure viewer or printed diagram; modeling materials.
idea: Give chemistry and biochemistry a concrete object in the study of mind.
steps: Locate the binding site and membrane channel in the model.
Arrange a sequence from transmitter binding to channel opening.
Mark the explanatory gap between this mechanism and a complete account of experience.
output: A molecular-to-cellular diagram with explicit scale labels.
note: A molecular model explains a mechanism, not consciousness as a whole. Use a physical or printed model when the viewer is inaccessible.

title: Read coordination without a brain
object: Levin and collaborators · information structures in aneural tissues
materials: Published figures; a small instructor-made network dataset.
idea: Connect living organization with the language of cognition.
steps: Identify what the study actually measures.
Draw a network from the sample dataset.
Separate measured coordination from a claim about felt experience.
output: An annotated network and two differently scoped claims.
note: The sample is an instructional model, not tissue data. No live biological experiment is proposed here.

source.label: Revealing non-trivial information structures in aneural biological tissues via functional connectivity

title: Compare performance with a claim to experience
object: Alan Turing · Computing Machinery and Intelligence
materials: Turing’s article; instructor-written illustrative transcripts.
idea: Make computing part of the common course without equating fluency with consciousness.
steps: Read Turing’s test proposal.
Compare two clearly labeled illustrative transcripts against stated criteria.
Write separate conclusions about performance and subjective experience.
output: A test specification with a limits statement.
note: Synthetic transcripts must be labeled. No private student writing needs to be sent to an AI system.

title: Take the notebook seriously
object: Clark & Chalmers · The Extended Mind
materials: Short paper excerpt; a notebook or task checklist.
idea: Bring everyday tools and accessibility into the philosophical account.
steps: Read the paper’s notebook example.
Complete a short planning task with an external checklist.
Diagram the roles played by person, tool and environment.
output: A system diagram and a passage-based argument.
note: This is an illustration of a disputed thesis, not a test proving that tools are conscious.

title: Make a record of directed attention
object: William James · attention; a campus soundwalk
materials: A brief James excerpt; a chosen accessible location; notebook.
idea: Let place, sound and attention enter the same observation.
steps: Listen briefly without a recording device.
Repeat while attending to one sound category.
Compare the two written inventories.
output: Two sound inventories with a note on the change of method.
note: Offer a stationary indoor location and a visual observation alternative. The exercise illustrates attention; it does not prove a restorative effect of nature.

source.label: William James · Principles of Psychology, chapter XI: Attention

title: Infer a mind from an object
object: Smithsonian · early tools, images and instruments
materials: Museum object records and images; material or replica examples if available.
idea: Connect archaeology, material evidence and the limits of interpretation.
steps: Choose one documented early object.
Describe its observable features before interpreting them.
Write separate labels for a supported capacity and an uncertain belief.
output: A two-part museum label distinguishing evidence and inference.
note: Do not present an object as a transcript of its maker’s beliefs or living peoples as replicas of prehistoric societies.

title: Compare observation and interpretation on a journey
object: Hyecho’s pilgrimage account · translation credited to Matty Wegehaupt and collaborators
materials: Authorized translated passage and the Michigan project’s context.
idea: Connect travel, religious practice and the limits of knowing other people.
steps: Read a short passage with its translation credit.
Mark direct observation separately from reported information and interpretation.
Compare the account with the project’s historical explanation.
output: A source-based annotation suitable for a small exhibition.
note: Confirm the edition and excerpt access. This is a proposal to use the published work, not an endorsement by the project’s contributors.

source.label: Hyecho’s pilgrimage account — translation and teaching context

title: Curate a campus history of attention
object: Lawrence’s Lux · public concert programs and archival collections
materials: Three public items selected from Lux with a librarian or archivist.
idea: Make the campus’s own intellectual and performance history part of MIND(s).
steps: Choose three public objects around one practice, such as recital preparation or collective listening.
Record creator, date, audience and context for each.
Write an exhibition introduction linking the objects through an explicit argument.
output: A three-object exhibition proposal.
note: The linked catalog identifies collections, not a preselected set of objects. Selection and reuse terms still need checking; no private records are included.

title: Observe attention during a short reading
object: Dhammapada · verses on mind
materials: A credited translation of verses 33–43; a neutral short prose passage.
idea: Pair a text on mental cultivation with a modest observation of attention.
steps: Read the selected verses in their Buddhist context.
Read the prose silently for two minutes, noting a return of attention if it occurs.
Distinguish the textual teaching from this classroom observation.
output: A private observation note and a textual annotation.
note: Participation can be textual only. This is not a therapeutic intervention or a complete Buddhist meditation practice.
